pages.text: The United Nations spoke about the war in Sudan in October. Rosemary DiCarlo told the Security Council that fighting was getting worse. Many people were suffering because of the conflict.
She said attacks on ordinary people and aid workers must stop. She also asked people involved in the fighting to stop using drones. The situation could affect nearby countries too.
The United Nations is trying to help people talk about peace. A UN envoy, Pekka Haavisto, is supporting talks about useful steps, including prisoner exchanges and access to education.
DiCarlo asked the sides to take talks seriously. She also called for a break in fighting so people could receive help. She said civilians should have a voice in the peace process.

The United Nations has warned that the conflict in Sudan is becoming more dangerous. Speaking to the Security Council on October 16, Under-Secretary-General Rosemary DiCarlo described escalating fighting and widespread suffering among civilians.

The warning also addressed the danger that violence could spread beyond Sudan. DiCarlo condemned attacks directed at civilians and humanitarian operations, emphasizing the damage that continuing hostilities can cause to affected communities.

She called on the parties to stop using drones and urged outside actors to help end the conflict rather than make it worse. Her remarks placed responsibility on both those fighting and those influencing the conflict.
Diplomatic activity is continuing. UN Personal Envoy Pekka Haavisto is working on confidence-building measures, including possible prisoner exchanges and efforts to improve access to education.

The UN called for a humanitarian truce and a wider political process involving civilians. The appeal described steps that could support negotiations, not an agreement that the parties have already reached.

Briefing the Security Council on October 16, United Nations Under-Secretary-General Rosemary DiCarlo warned that Sudan’s conflict was intensifying, with severe consequences for civilians and growing risks of instability spreading across the region.

Her assessment highlighted the breadth of the humanitarian crisis rather than treating the violence as an isolated military confrontation. Attacks on civilians and humanitarian operations formed a central part of the concerns she raised.
DiCarlo called for an end to the use of drones by the warring parties. She also urged external actors to support efforts to halt the conflict instead of contributing to its continuation.

The diplomatic track remains active, according to the UN account. Personal Envoy Pekka Haavisto has been pursuing confidence-building initiatives, among them prisoner exchanges and improved access to education.

Such measures are intended to create a more workable environment for broader negotiations. They should not be mistaken for evidence that a nationwide ceasefire or comprehensive political settlement has already been secured.

The United Nations urged a humanitarian truce and inclusive, civilian-led political efforts. DiCarlo called on the parties to demonstrate credible commitment to talks while encouraging the Security Council to use its available tools to help end the war.

pages.text: The World Bank Group and Japan are working together on energy problems in Asia. They announced a first project under a plan called DRIVE on October 15.
The new project is part of a larger partnership. It aims to make energy supplies safer and help countries deal with problems in the supply of important goods.
The World Bank Group says the partnership also hopes to bring more private investment to Asia. That means encouraging companies to put money into useful projects.
The plan also aims to create jobs and support economic growth over time. The announcement explains what the partners want to do, but it does not say that every result has already happened.

The World Bank Group announced the first project under its DRIVE framework in cooperation with Japan. The announcement, made in Bangkok on October 15, focuses on improving energy and supply-chain resilience across Asia.

The framework is designed to help countries respond to disruptions in energy markets and important supply chains. Its name refers to the Dynamic Response for Invigorating Value Chains and Energy Security initiative.

Energy resilience matters because interruptions to supplies can put pressure on businesses and economies. The World Bank Group presents the project as part of a partnership intended to help countries prepare for those risks.
The initiative also aims to attract private investment. Involving private companies is one possible way to support business activity and develop stronger value chains in the region.
The partners identify job creation and long-term economic growth among the intended benefits. These are goals of the initiative, not results that the announcement says have already been achieved.
The World Bank Group and Japan announced the first project developed under the DRIVE framework on October 15, presenting it as a step toward greater energy and supply-chain resilience across Asia.

DRIVE stands for Dynamic Response for Invigorating Value Chains and Energy Security. The framework addresses vulnerabilities that can arise when economies depend on supplies of energy and other essential inputs.

The World Bank Group positions the initiative as part of a broader effort to strengthen countries’ capacity to manage disruption. Its stated purpose includes more reliable access to energy and stronger regional value chains.

Another objective is to mobilize private investment. The announcement links that ambition to job creation and greater economic activity, while making clear that the project represents an initiative rather than a completed transformation.

Energy security and supply-chain performance have implications beyond the energy sector. Interruptions can affect production and investment decisions, which helps explain why an institution focused on development is involved.

The announcement therefore sets out a prospective development agenda: improving resilience, encouraging investment and supporting long-term growth. Assessing the eventual impact will require evidence of implementation and results that the initial announcement does not yet provide.

pages.text: Nepal and the World Bank Group want to look at a new way to prepare for earthquakes. They signed an agreement on October 15 to study a type of financial protection.
The idea is called a catastrophe bond. It could help Nepal receive money quickly after a major earthquake. Faster access to money can matter when a country is dealing with a disaster.
The agreement does not mean Nepal has already sold such a bond. It means the two sides will study whether the idea could work and what the bond might look like.
Nepal faces serious risks from natural disasters. The World Bank says the study is part of a wider plan to help the country prepare, reduce risks and protect public finances.
Nepal and the World Bank Group have agreed to explore a catastrophe bond as a possible tool for earthquake protection. They signed a mandate agreement in Bangkok on October 15.

A catastrophe bond can help a country gain access to funds after a major natural disaster. In this case, the proposed instrument is being considered as a way to provide Nepal with financial support quickly after a severe earthquake.

The agreement begins an assessment rather than launching a completed bond. The World Bank Group Treasury will work with Nepal’s government and financial-market participants to examine whether the transaction is feasible.
They will also consider how such a bond could be structured. These decisions are important because any financial arrangement must be suitable for the risks that the country aims to manage.

The initiative sits within Nepal’s wider disaster-risk strategy, which includes prevention, preparedness and financial protection. The World Bank Group describes catastrophe bonds as a way for countries to share some disaster risks with international capital markets.

Nepal and the World Bank Group signed a mandate agreement on October 15 to explore the feasibility of a catastrophe bond designed to strengthen the country’s financial preparedness for major earthquakes.

Unlike conventional borrowing arrangements, catastrophe bonds are intended to transfer specified disaster risks to investors. The World Bank Group says such instruments can provide access to financial resources when severe natural hazards occur.

The announcement should be understood as an exploratory step. No completed catastrophe-bond issuance was announced; the agreement instead authorizes work on the transaction’s potential structure and viability.

World Bank Group Treasury will engage with Nepalese authorities and relevant market participants. Their analysis is expected to inform whether a financial instrument of this kind can complement existing risk-management arrangements.

Nepal’s exposure to earthquakes makes financial preparedness particularly important. The country’s broader approach combines disaster-risk reduction, planning and measures intended to strengthen protection against future losses.

The proposed partnership illustrates how international capital markets may form part of sovereign disaster-risk strategies. Its practical value, however, remains contingent on the feasibility assessment and on any subsequent decisions to proceed.

pages.text: The International Monetary Fund planned a meeting about artificial intelligence and the world economy on October 16. People often call artificial intelligence AI. It can change how people learn and work.
The meeting was part of the IMF annual events in Bangkok. The program asked how businesses can use AI and what new problems the technology could bring.
AI may help some companies work faster. But people also have questions about jobs and skills. The IMF program said leaders needed to think about both possible benefits and risks.
The meeting also planned to discuss money, cyber risks and the future of work. Its program asked how different countries could benefit from AI without leaving people behind.

The International Monetary Fund scheduled a seminar on artificial intelligence and the global economy for October 16 during its annual meetings in Bangkok. The program focused on how AI is changing businesses, employment and economic policy.

The event, titled AI and the Global Economy: From Risk to Opportunity, was designed to explore new opportunities for productivity and growth. It also examined the challenges caused by rapid technological change.
Among the themes listed by the IMF were labor markets, international supply chains and competitiveness. These subjects reflect the fact that AI can influence more than technology companies alone.
The agenda also included financial stability, cyber risks and market concentration. Such concerns matter because powerful new tools may bring economic benefits while creating new vulnerabilities.

The program highlighted policy choices that could help workers gain new skills and allow more countries to benefit. These were discussion topics announced by the IMF, not final policy decisions or demonstrated outcomes.

The International Monetary Fund organized its annual-meetings program around a seminar scheduled for October 16 on the economic implications of artificial intelligence, entitled AI and the Global Economy: From Risk to Opportunity.

The agenda framed AI as a technology already influencing production, business operations and labor markets. It invited consideration of productivity gains alongside the institutional and distributional challenges associated with accelerating adoption.

Participants were expected to examine how businesses deploy AI to improve efficiency and how the technology affects global value chains, investment and competitiveness. These issues connect technological change to macroeconomic performance.

The IMF program also identified cyber threats, financial-stability risks and market concentration as matters requiring scrutiny. Economic opportunities do not remove the need to consider vulnerabilities arising from new technologies.

A further focus was the policy environment: innovation incentives, workforce skills and the ability of different economies to participate in AI-driven growth. The program paid particular attention to Asia-Pacific economies undergoing digital transformation.

The published material describes the purpose and scheduled discussion topics of the forum. It should not be interpreted as evidence that the participants reached specific agreements or that the projected benefits of AI have already materialized.
